pages.subtitle: A rich young man who gave up everything to follow Jesus and care for the poor.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Living simply, serving the poor, and praising God for all creation

pages.intro: Francis was born into a rich family in Assisi, Italy, more than 800 years ago. As a young man, he dreamed of becoming a knight. Then he gave everything away to live like Jesus, poor and close to people in need. Other men joined him, and they became known as the Franciscans. Francis praised God for the sun, the moon, and every living creature.
story_paragraphs: Francis was born in the town of Assisi, Italy, in 1181 or 1182. His father, Pietro, was a rich cloth merchant. The baby was baptized Giovanni, but his father called him Francesco, and that is the name we remember. Young Francis had a carefree life and dreamed of becoming a knight.

In 1202, Francis fought in a war between Assisi and the nearby city of Perugia. He was captured and held as a prisoner for almost a year. After he was freed, he became very sick. Slowly, Francis began to change. One day he met a man with leprosy, a disease that people feared. Francis gave him money and kissed his hand.
Around 1205, Francis was praying in a small, broken-down church called San Damiano. There he heard Jesus speak to him from the cross: "Go, Francis, and repair my Church in ruins."

Francis's father was angry that his son gave so much to the poor. In front of the bishop of Assisi, Francis gave back everything he had from his father, even his clothes. From then on, he owned nothing. He begged for what he needed and preached about turning back to God.

Soon other men joined him. In 1209, Francis wrote a simple rule of life for them. He led twelve followers to Rome, and Pope Innocent III gave his approval. They became known as the Friars Minor, or Franciscans. In 1212, a young noblewoman named Clare joined Francis, and a community for women began.

In 1219, during a war, Francis traveled to Egypt and walked into the camp of the Muslim sultan, al-Kamil, to speak with him. At Christmas in 1223, in the town of Greccio, Francis asked a friend to prepare a manger with hay, an ox, and a donkey, so people could picture the night Jesus was born.

Francis called all creatures his brothers and sisters. In 1224, while praying at a quiet place called La Verna, he received the stigmata, wounds like the wounds of Jesus. In his last years, Francis was very sick and had lost much of his sight.
Francis died on the evening of October 3, 1226, at a little chapel called the Portiuncula. Two years later, Pope Gregory IX declared him a saint.

At Greccio in 1223, there were no statues in the manger scene. The people who came took part in it themselves.
Francis wrote a song called the Canticle of the Creatures. In it, he praises God for "Brother Sun" and "Sister Moon."
Old stories tell of Francis preaching to the birds and making peace between a wolf and the town of Gubbio.
In 1979, Pope John Paul II named Francis the patron saint of ecology, which is the care of nature.
Francis is one of the patron saints of Italy.

canonical.match_title: St. Thérèse of Lisieux (Little Flower of Jesus)

pages.subtitle: A young sister who showed that small things done with great love matter to God.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Her "little way" of trust and love

pages.intro: Thérèse Martin grew up in France in a family that loved God. When she was only 15, she became a Carmelite sister in the town of Lisieux. She did not do anything famous. Instead, she offered small, everyday things to Jesus with great love. She called this her "little way." Thérèse died when she was just 24, and the Church honors her as a great teacher.
story_paragraphs: Thérèse Martin was born on January 2, 1873, in Alençon, France. Her parents were Louis and Zélie Martin. Thérèse was the youngest in the family, and she had four older sisters.

When Thérèse was four years old, her mother died. The family moved to the town of Lisieux. A few years later, Thérèse became seriously ill. On Pentecost in 1883, she was healed, and she thanked Mary for praying for her.

Thérèse wanted to give her whole life to God as a Carmelite sister, like her older sisters Pauline and Marie. Carmelites live in a convent and spend their days in prayer. But Thérèse was told she was too young. On November 20, 1887, during a trip to Rome, she asked Pope Leo XIII himself to let her enter at age 15.

On April 9, 1888, Thérèse entered the Carmelite convent in Lisieux. She was 15 years old. She became Sister Thérèse of the Child Jesus and the Holy Face. Two years later, she made her vows, her promises to God.

Thérèse found a simple way to grow close to God. She trusted him the way a small child trusts a loving parent, and she offered him little sacrifices each day. She called it the "little way." She said it was "the way of trust and absolute surrender." She taught it to the newest sisters.
The leaders of the convent asked Thérèse to write down the story of her life, and she began in 1895.

Then Thérèse became sick with tuberculosis, a serious illness of the lungs. During this time she wrote in a letter, "I am not dying, I am entering life." Thérèse died on September 30, 1897. She was 24 years old. Her last words were, "My God, I love you!"

In 1898, her writings were printed as a book called Story of a Soul. Pope Pius XI declared her a saint on May 17, 1925. In 1997, Pope John Paul II named her a Doctor of the Church, a title for saints whose teaching helps the whole Church.

pages.subtitle: A humble Native man from Mexico who carried Mary's message to his bishop.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Bringing Our Lady of Guadalupe's message to the bishop

pages.intro: Juan Diego was a Native man who lived in Mexico about 500 years ago. In December 1531, on a hill called Tepeyac, Mary appeared to him and asked for a church to be built there. The bishop asked for a sign. Juan Diego brought him roses in his cloak, and an image of Mary appeared on the cloth. That image is still honored today.
story_paragraphs: Juan Diego was born in 1474 in Cuautitlán, in the land we now call Mexico. His Native name was Cuauhtlatoatzin, which means "the Talking Eagle." He belonged to the Chichimeca people.
In 1524, Franciscan missionaries came to Mexico to teach people about Jesus. Juan Diego and his wife, María Lucía, were among the first Native people there to be baptized. María Lucía died in 1529.

According to the tradition handed down for almost 500 years, Juan Diego was walking to Mass on December 9, 1531. As he crossed a hill called Tepeyac, Mary appeared to him. She asked him to go to the bishop and ask for a church to be built on the hill.
Juan Diego went to Bishop Juan de Zumárraga. The bishop listened and asked him questions. Then he asked for a sign to show that the message was true.

Soon after, Juan Diego's uncle, Juan Bernardino, became very sick. On December 12, Juan Diego went looking for a priest to help him. Mary appeared again. She told Juan Diego that his uncle would get well. Then she told him to gather the flowers he would find on the hill and take them to the bishop. It was winter, yet roses were blooming there. Juan Diego carried them in his cloak, called a tilma.
Juan Diego opened his tilma in front of the bishop. The roses fell out, and an image of Mary could be seen on the cloth. The bishop ordered a church to be built on Tepeyac Hill.
Juan Diego spent the rest of his life in a small home beside that church. He lived simply and cared for the pilgrims who came to pray. He died in 1548.

Pope John Paul II declared Juan Diego a saint on July 31, 2002. He was the first Indigenous person of the Americas to be made a saint. His tilma, with the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe, is still kept in her basilica in Mexico City.

pages.subtitle: A young Mohawk woman who followed Jesus with courage.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Ossernenon, a Mohawk village in what is now New York

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Her courage and her life of prayer

pages.intro: Kateri Tekakwitha was a Mohawk woman born in 1656 in what is now the state of New York. When she was four, a sickness called smallpox took her family and left her with scars and weak eyes. At age 20, she chose to be baptized. Later she traveled a long way to a Christian village in Canada, where she gave her days to prayer.
story_paragraphs: Tekakwitha was born in 1656 in Ossernenon, a Mohawk village in what is now the state of New York. Her father was a Mohawk chief. Her mother was an Algonquin woman and a Christian.

Those were hard years for her people. When Tekakwitha was about four, a sickness called smallpox spread through the village. Her mother, her father, and her little brother all died. Tekakwitha lived, but the sickness left scars on her face and hurt her eyes. Her uncle, a village chief, took her in.

In 1666, French soldiers burned the Mohawk villages. The people built a new village across the river. The next year, three Jesuit priests came to stay for a few days, and Tekakwitha helped take care of them.

Tekakwitha grew up skilled at beadwork and basket weaving. Her family expected her to marry, but she wished to stay unmarried. Later, a priest named Father Jacques de Lamberville taught her about the Catholic faith. On Easter Sunday in 1676, when she was 20, she was baptized. She was given the name Catherine. In the Mohawk language, the name is Kateri.

Her uncle was against the Christian faith. After her baptism, some people in the village treated Kateri cruelly, and she was even threatened. In the fall of 1677, she left with three other Native Christians. They traveled a very long way to the Mission of Saint Francis Xavier, near the city of Montreal in Canada.

At the mission, Kateri received her First Holy Communion on Christmas Day, 1677. She went to Mass every day and gave much of her time to prayer. On March 25, 1679, she made a promise to belong to Jesus alone for the rest of her life.

Kateri became very sick. She died on April 17, 1680, when she was about 24 years old, saying the names of Jesus and Mary. A priest who was there wrote that her scarred face became beautiful soon after she died.
Pope Benedict XVI declared Kateri a saint on October 21, 2012. She is the first Indigenous woman of North America to be named a saint.

pages.subtitle: Known around the world as Mother Teresa, she gave her life to caring for the poorest of the poor.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Skopje (now in North Macedonia); served in Calcutta, India

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Caring for the poorest of the poor

pages.intro: Mother Teresa was a Catholic sister who spent most of her life in Calcutta, a big city in India. She left her work as a school principal to live among the poorest people in the city. She cared for people who had no one else to care for them. Other women joined her, and they became the Missionaries of Charity. In 2016, Pope Francis declared her a saint.
story_paragraphs: Mother Teresa was born on August 26, 1910, in the city of Skopje. Her name was Gonxha Agnes Bojaxhiu, and she was the youngest child in her family. When she was about eight years old, her father died suddenly, and life became harder for the family.

At age 18, Agnes left home to become a missionary. In September 1928, she joined the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland. A few months later she traveled to India, and she arrived in Calcutta on January 6, 1929. She took a new name, Sister Teresa, after Saint Thérèse of Lisieux.
For many years, Sister Teresa taught at Saint Mary's School for girls in Calcutta. In 1944, she became the principal.

On September 10, 1946, Sister Teresa was riding a train to the town of Darjeeling. On that trip, she felt Jesus calling her to leave the convent school and serve the poorest people. She called it her "call within a call."

On August 17, 1948, she put on a simple white sari with a blue border and walked out into the city. She started an outdoor school for children in the poorest neighborhoods, called slums. She cared for people who were sick, hungry, and alone.

Other women came to help. On October 7, 1950, her new religious family, the Missionaries of Charity, officially began. Their work was to love and care for people nobody else was ready to look after. The sisters spread to many countries. In 1979, Mother Teresa was given the Nobel Peace Prize.
Mother Teresa also carried a hidden sorrow. For many years, when she prayed, she felt as if God were far away. She called it "the darkness." She kept praying and serving anyway.

Mother Teresa died on September 5, 1997. By that year, there were nearly 4,000 Missionaries of Charity sisters, serving in 123 countries. On September 4, 2016, Pope Francis declared her a saint in St. Peter's Square in Rome.

pages.subtitle: A boy taken from his home who later went back to share the faith with the people of Ireland.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Sharing the Christian faith across Ireland

pages.intro: Patrick lived about 1,600 years ago. When he was about 16, raiders took him from his home in Britain and sold him as a slave in Ireland. For six years he watched over sheep and prayed. After he escaped, he chose to go back to Ireland as a bishop to teach the people about Jesus. Today he is the patron saint of Ireland.
story_paragraphs: Patrick was born in Britain when it was part of the Roman Empire. His father, Calpornius, was a deacon, and his grandfather, Potitus, was a priest. We know these things because Patrick wrote about his own life. His story begins with the words, "My name is Patrick."
When Patrick was about 16, raiders from Ireland attacked his home. They carried him across the sea and sold him as a slave. For six years, Patrick worked in Ireland taking care of sheep.
Patrick was far from home, and he turned to God. He wrote that he prayed up to one hundred times in a day, and almost as many times at night.

One night in a dream, Patrick heard a voice say, "Look – your ship is ready." He ran away from the man who held him as a slave. He traveled about two hundred miles to reach the ship. After a hard journey, Patrick finally came home to his family.

Later, Patrick had another dream. A man named Victoricus came from Ireland carrying many letters. As Patrick read one, he seemed to hear the voice of the Irish people calling, "We beg you, holy boy, to come and walk again among us."

Patrick prepared for years, and he was made a bishop. Around the year 432, he went back to Ireland, the land where he had been a slave. For about thirty years, he taught people about Jesus and baptized them.
Patrick also stood up for people who were hurt. When soldiers attacked Irish Christians and carried some of them off as slaves, Patrick wrote a strong letter against it.

It is said that Patrick died at a place called Saul, in what is now Northern Ireland. Later, people told many legends about him. One says he used a three-leaf plant, the shamrock, to teach about the Holy Trinity. Another says he drove all the snakes out of Ireland.

timeline.text: Patrick is born in Roman Britain. No one knows the exact year.
Raiders take Patrick to Ireland and sell him as a slave.
After a dream, Patrick escapes and travels about two hundred miles to a ship.
In a dream, Patrick hears the Irish people asking him to come back.

Patrick teaches and baptizes people across Ireland.
The Church celebrates the feast of Saint Patrick every year.

fun_facts: Patrick was not born in Ireland. He was born in Britain.
Two of Patrick's own writings still exist: the story of his life, called the Confessio, and a letter.
As a young shepherd, Patrick prayed up to one hundred times a day.
Patrick traveled about two hundred miles to reach the ship that took him away from Ireland.
The story of Patrick and the shamrock is a legend, and so is the story about the snakes.

A person who is owned by someone else and forced to work without freedom. Slavery is a great wrong.
A leader in the Church who cares for all the Christians in an area.
An old story that many people tell, which may not have happened just the way it is told.
The Christian belief that there is one God in three Persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

pages.subtitle: A kind bishop from long ago whose secret gifts are still remembered every December.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Myra, in what is now Turkey

pages.intro: Saint Nicholas was a bishop who lived about 1,700 years ago in Myra, a town in the land we now call Turkey. We know very little about his life for certain. But for hundreds of years, people have told stories about his kindness, especially about the secret gifts he gave to people in need. Those stories even helped shape the story of Santa Claus.
story_paragraphs: Saint Nicholas lived so long ago that almost no records of his life remain. Historians say the one thing we can be fairly sure of is that he was the bishop of Myra in the 300s. Myra was a town in what is now the country of Turkey. Everything else comes from tradition, which means stories handed down over many years.

According to tradition, Nicholas was born in a seaport town called Patara. His parents were wealthy, and they raised him to love God. They died in an epidemic, a sickness that spread to many people, while Nicholas was still young. The stories say Nicholas used all the money they left him to help people who were poor, sick, or suffering.

Nicholas became the bishop of Myra while he was still a young man. In those days, the Roman emperor Diocletian was arresting Christians. Tradition says Nicholas was put in prison for his faith and was set free under the next emperor, Constantine.

The most famous story about Nicholas tells of a poor man with three daughters. The father had no money for a dowry, which a young woman needed in order to marry. Without it, the daughters faced a very hard life. On three different nights, a bag of gold was tossed through an open window. The story says the gold landed in stockings or shoes left by the fire to dry.
Other stories tell of Nicholas praying during a storm at sea until the waves grew calm. That is why sailors ask for his prayers.
Nicholas was buried in his church at Myra. In 1087, Italian sailors carried his remains to the city of Bari, Italy, where they are still kept.

In Holland, people called him Sinterklaas. Dutch families brought their stories about him to America in the 1600s. There, the name slowly turned into "Santa Claus." In many countries, children still receive small gifts on Saint Nicholas Day, December 6.

timeline.text: According to tradition, Nicholas is born in the seaport of Patara.
Nicholas serves as bishop of Myra. Tradition says he is put in prison for his faith and later set free.
Tradition holds that Nicholas died on this day. It became his feast.
His tomb in Myra is well known, and a church is built in his honor in the great city of Constantinople.

The American picture of Santa Claus takes shape.

fun_facts: The name "Santa Claus" comes from Sinterklaas, the Dutch name for Saint Nicholas.
In the old story, the bags of gold landed in stockings or shoes drying by the fire.
In the Netherlands, children leave carrots and hay in their shoes for Saint Nicholas's horse.
Saint Nicholas is honored as a patron saint of children and of sailors.
Greece and Russia both honor Saint Nicholas as a patron saint.

pages.subtitle: A boy from Poland who became pope and told the whole world, "Do not be afraid!"

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Serving as pope for more than 26 years and bringing the faith to people all over the world

pages.intro: Karol Wojtyła grew up in a small town in Poland. By the time he was 20, he had lost his mother, his brother, and his father. During a terrible war, he studied in secret to become a priest. In 1978, he was chosen as pope and took the name John Paul II. He visited 129 countries and told people everywhere, "Do not be afraid!"
story_paragraphs: Karol Wojtyła was born on May 18, 1920, in Wadowice, Poland. He was the youngest of three children. His friends called him Lolek.

Karol knew sadness early in his life. His mother died in 1929, when he was eight. His older brother, Edmund, who was a doctor, died in 1932. His father died in 1941. At age 20, Karol had lost his whole family.

In 1938, Karol began studying at the university in the city of Kraków. He loved acting in plays. But in 1939, the army of Nazi Germany took over Poland and closed the university. To earn a living, and to keep from being sent away to Germany, Karol worked in a stone quarry and then in a chemical factory.

In 1942, Karol felt God calling him to be a priest. The seminary, a school for future priests, had to meet in secret. He also helped run a secret theater. Karol was ordained a priest on November 1, 1946. Father Karol became a teacher, then a bishop in 1958, the archbishop of Kraków in 1964, and a cardinal in 1967.
On October 16, 1978, the cardinals elected him pope. He took the name John Paul II. He was the first pope from outside Italy in 455 years. As he began, he told the world, "Do not be afraid!"
Pope John Paul II made 104 trips outside Italy and visited 129 countries. He started World Youth Day, a great gathering for young people.
On May 13, 1981, a man shot the Pope in St. Peter's Square. John Paul II survived. In 1983, he went to the prison to visit the man who had shot him, and he forgave him.
John Paul II died on April 2, 2005. Pope Francis declared him a saint on April 27, 2014, together with Pope John XXIII.

timeline.text: Karol Wojtyła is born in Wadowice, Poland.
Nazi Germany takes over Poland and closes Karol's university. He goes to work in a quarry.
Karol begins studying in secret to become a priest.
Karol is ordained a priest in Kraków.
